notes.meaning: King Josiah celebrated the Passover in Jerusalem to worship the Lord. The Passover lamb was killed on the exact day required by the Law of Moses, the fourteenth day of the first month. Unlike earlier kings who had to delay the feast, Josiah was able to hold it at the proper appointed time. Faithful obedience means following God's timing and directions carefully.

Josiah assigned the priests to their specific duties in the temple. He encouraged them with kind words so they would serve with joy and confidence. Good leaders help others find their place and cheer them on in God's work.

Josiah told the Levites to place the sacred ark of the covenant back into Solomon's temple. Because the ark had a permanent home, the Levites no longer needed to carry it on their shoulders. Instead, they were freed to teach God's law to the people and care for their spiritual needs.

The king instructed the Levites to organize themselves by their family divisions. They were told to follow the written plans that King David and King Solomon had established long before. God desires His house and worship to be ordered and peaceful.

Josiah told the Levites to stand ready in the temple courts. Each group of Levites was assigned to assist a specific family group of ordinary citizens. This teamwork ensured that every household received the guidance and help they needed to worship.

The Levites were ordered to make themselves ceremonially clean and slaughter the Passover lambs. Because many regular people had not had time to purify themselves, the Levites stepped in to help them follow Moses' law. Serving others often means doing extra work so everyone can draw near to God.

Josiah gave thirty thousand lambs and young goats, along with three thousand cattle, from his own royal herds to provide for the crowd. Many families were too poor to bring their own animals after years of hardship. The king made sure no one was left out of the feast.

The king's leading temple administrators followed his example and gave freely to the priests and Levites. Leaders like Hilkiah provided thousands of sheep and goats and hundreds of cattle. Generosity at the top encouraged other leaders to share their wealth gladly.

Prominent Levite leaders also donated five thousand small animals and five hundred cattle to their fellow Levites. They made sure the working ministers had plenty of food and offerings for the celebration. God's servants should always look out for one another's needs.

All the preparations were complete, and the priests and Levites stood at their stations. Everyone took their proper place just as the king had directed. Thorough preparation leads to reverent and peaceful worship.

The Levites slaughtered the Passover animals and removed the skins. They handed the blood to the priests, who sprinkled it against the altar. The Levites handled these heavy tasks because the number of sacrifices was so large.

The workers separated the parts meant for burnt offerings from the meat meant for the meal. These portions were offered to God exactly as written in the Book of Moses. They treated both the sheep and the cattle with the same careful obedience.

The priests and Levites roasted the Passover lambs over the fire as the law commanded. They boiled the other peace offerings in pots and kettles and brought the meat quickly to the people. Serving the food right away helped everyone eat without delay and recalled the urgency of the first Passover.

After serving the worshippers, the Levites prepared food for themselves and for the priests. The priests were busy burning sacrifices and fat on the altar until night fell. Caring for others first is a wonderful picture of Christian service.

The musicians stayed at their posts singing praises, and the gatekeepers guarded the doors without leaving their stations. Fellow Levites brought meals directly to them so they could stay focused on their duties. When believers support one another, the whole church functions smoothly.

The entire Passover service and the offerings on the altar were completed that day, just as Josiah had commanded. Everything was carried out in full agreement with God's law. The people enjoyed a complete day of faithful worship.

All the people of Israel who were present kept the Passover and then celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days. They continued praising God together for an entire week. Remembering God's rescue should lead to ongoing thanksgiving and joy.

No Passover like this one had been celebrated since the time of Samuel the prophet. It stood out because of the king's unmatched generosity, the deep devotion of the people, and their strict obedience to God's written commands. Wholehearted obedience brings special joy to God's people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view Josiah's festival as establishing an enduring, legally ordered institution with fixed roles, rather than being an informal gathering.

notes.meaning: This magnificent Passover took place in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign. It marked the high point of his work to repair the temple and bring the nation back to God.

Years later, after Josiah had restored the temple worship, Pharaoh Neco of Egypt marched north to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates River. King Josiah chose to march out with his army to block Neco's advance. Even after seasons of faithfulness, difficult trials can unexpectedly appear.

Neco sent messengers explaining that he had no quarrel with Judah and was only rushing to fight another kingdom. He told Josiah that God had commanded him to hurry and warned the king not to interfere. God can choose to speak a warning even through a foreign ruler.

Josiah refused to turn back and disguised himself in armor so he could fight on the plain of Megiddo. He failed to ask the Lord for direction and ignored the true warning that came through Neco. Rushing into a conflict without prayer and counsel leads to disaster.

During the battle, Egyptian archers shot King Josiah. Wounded badly, the king told his servants to carry him away from the fight. A person cannot hide from God's sovereign will, no matter what disguise they wear.

His servants moved Josiah into his second chariot and brought him back to Jerusalem, where he died. He was buried in the royal tombs, and the entire nation wept bitterly over his death. The people realized they had lost a truly good and loving shepherd.

The prophet Jeremiah composed funeral poems for Josiah, and singing choirs continued to sing these laments for generations. The songs were recorded in a collection of mourning poems and became a regular tradition in Israel. Losing a godly ruler leaves deep sorrow in a nation's heart.

The rest of Josiah's deeds and his acts of faithful love were recorded in accordance with God's law. He lived a life marked by steadfast devotion to the Lord and kindness to his people. A life shaped by God's Word leaves behind an honorable legacy.

All the events of Josiah's life, from his earliest days to his death, were recorded in the official history of the kings of Israel and Judah. His entire life was remembered so future generations could learn from his example.
